name: Practical skills: planning, analysis and evaluation

statementText.1.1.1(a): experimental design, including to solve problems set in a practical context
statementText.1.1.1(b): identification of variables that must be controlled, where appropriate
statementText.1.1.1(c): evaluation that an experimental method is appropriate to meet the expected outcomes.
statementText.1.1.2(a): how to use a wide range of practical apparatus and techniques correctly
statementText.1.1.2(c): presenting observations and data in an appropriate format.
statementText.1.1.3(a): processing, analysing and interpreting qualitative and quantitative experimental results
statementText.1.1.3(b): use of appropriate mathematical skills for analysis of quantitative data
statementText.1.1.3(d): plotting and interpreting suitable graphs from experimental results, including:
statementText.1.1.3(d)(i): selection and labelling of axes with appropriate scales, quantities and units
statementText.1.1.4(a): how to evaluate results and draw conclusions
statementText.1.1.4(b): the identification of anomalies in experimental measurements
statementText.1.1.4(d): precision and accuracy of measurements and data, including margins of error, percentage errors and uncertainties in apparatus
statementText.1.1.4(e): refining experimental design by suggestion of improvements to the procedures and apparatus.

statementText.1.2.1(a): apply investigative approaches and methods to practical work
statementText.1.2.1(b): safely and correctly use a range of practical equipment and materials
statementText.1.2.1(e): keep appropriate records of experimental activities
statementText.1.2.1(f): present information and data in a scientific way
statementText.1.2.1(g): use appropriate software and tools to process data, carry out research and report findings
statementText.1.2.1(h): use online and offline research skills including websites, textbooks and other printed scientific sources of information
statementText.1.2.1(j): use a wide range of experimental and practical instruments, equipment and techniques appropriate to the knowledge and understanding included in the specification.
statementText.1.2.2(a): use of appropriate apparatus to record a range of measurements (to include mass, time, volume of liquids and gases, temperature)
statementText.1.2.2(b): use of a water bath or electric heater or sand bath for heating
statementText.1.2.2(c): measurement of pH using pH charts, or pH meter, or pH probe on a data logger
statementText.1.2.2(d): use of laboratory apparatus for a variety of experimental techniques including:
statementText.1.2.2(d)(ii): distillation and heating under reflux, including setting up glassware using retort stand and clamps
statementText.1.2.2(d)(iii): qualitative tests for ions and organic functional groups
statementText.1.2.2(d)(iv): filtration, including use of fluted filter paper, or filtration under reduced pressure
statementText.1.2.2(e): use of a volumetric flask, including accurate technique for making up a standard solution
statementText.1.2.2(f): use of acid– base indicators in titrations of weak/ strong acids with weak/strong alkalis
statementText.1.2.2(g)(ii): a liquid product, including use of a separating funnel
statementText.1.2.2(i): use of thin layer or paper chromatography
statementText.1.2.2(j): setting up of electrochemical cells and measuring voltages
statementText.1.2.2(k): safely and carefully handling solids and liquids, including corrosive, irritant, flammable and toxic substances
statementText.1.2.2(l): measurement of rates of reaction by at least two different methods, for example:
statementText.1.2.2(l)(i): an initial rate method such as a clock reaction

statementText.2.1.1(a): isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons and different masses
statementText.2.1.1(b): atomic structure in terms of the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons for atoms and ions, given the atomic number, mass number and any ionic charge
statementText.2.1.1(c): explanation of the terms relative isotopic mass (mass compared with 1/12th mass of carbon-12) and relative atomic mass (weighted mean mass compared with 1/12th mass of carbon-12), based on the mass of a12C atom, the standard for atomic masses
statementText.2.1.1(d)(i): the determination of relative isotopic masses and relative abundances of the isotope,
statementText.2.1.1(d)(ii): calculation of the relative atomic mass of an element from the relative abundances of its isotopes
statementText.2.1.1(e): use of the terms relative molecular mass, Mr, and relative formula mass and their calculation from relative atomic masses.

statementText.2.1.2(a): the writing of formulae of ionic compounds from ionic charges, including:
statementText.2.1.2(a)(i): prediction of ionic charge from the position of an element in the periodic table
statementText.2.1.2(a)(ii): recall of the names and formulae for the following ions: NO3–, CO32–, SO42–, OH–, NH4+, Zn2+ and Ag+
statementText.2.1.2(b): construction of balanced chemical equations (including ionic equations), including state symbols, for reactions studied and for unfamiliar reactions given appropriate information.

statementText.2.1.3(a): explanation and use of the terms:
statementText.2.1.3(a)(ii): mole (symbol ‘mol’), as the unit for amount of substance
statementText.2.1.3(a)(iii): the Avogadro constant, NA(the number of particles per mole, 6.02 × 1023mol–1)
statementText.2.1.3(a)(iv): molar mass (mass per mole, units g mol–1),
statementText.2.1.3(a)(v): molar gas volume (gas volume per mole, units dm3mol–1)
statementText.2.1.3(b)(i): empirical formula (the simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element present in a compound)
statementText.2.1.3(b)(ii): molecular formula (the number and type of atoms of each element in a molecule)
statementText.2.1.3(c): calculations of empirical and molecular formulae, from composition by mass or percentage compositions by mass and relative molecular mass
statementText.2.1.3(d): the terms anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation and calculation of the formula of a hydrated salt from given percentage composition, mass composition or based on experimental results
statementText.2.1.3(e): calculations, using amount of substance in mol, involving:
statementText.2.1.3(f): the ideal gas equation: pV = nRT
statementText.2.1.3(g): use of stoichiometric relationships in calculations
statementText.2.1.3(h)(i): the percentage yield of a reaction or related quantities
statementText.2.1.3(h)(ii): the atom economy of a reaction
statementText.2.1.3(i): the techniques and procedures required during experiments requiring the measurement of mass, volumes of solutions and gas volumes
statementText.2.1.3(j): the benefits for sustainability of developing chemical processes with a high atom economy.

statementText.2.1.4(a): the formulae of the common acids (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3and CH3COOH) and the common alkalis (NaOH, KOH and NH3) and explanation that acids release H+ ions in aqueous solution and alkalis release OH– ions in aqueous solution
statementText.2.1.4(b): qualitative explanation of strong and weak acids in terms of relative dissociations
statementText.2.1.4(c)(i): H+ and OH– to form H2O
statementText.2.1.4(c)(ii): acids with bases, including carbonates, metal oxides and alkalis (water-soluble bases), to form salts, including full equations
statementText.2.1.4(d): the techniques and procedures used when preparing a standard solution of required concentration and carrying out acid– base titrations
statementText.2.1.4(e): structured and non-structured titration calculations, based on experimental results of familiar and non-familiar acids and bases.

statementText.2.1.5(a): rules for assigning and calculating oxidation number for atoms in elements, compounds and ions
statementText.2.1.5(c): use of a Roman numeral to indicate the magnitude of the oxidation number when an element may have compounds/ions with different oxidation numbers
statementText.2.1.5(d): oxidation and reduction in terms of:
statementText.2.1.5(e): redox reactions of metals with acids to form salts, including full equations (see also 2.1.4 c)
statementText.2.1.5(f): interpretation of redox equations in (e), and unfamiliar redox reactions, to make predictions in terms of oxidation numbers and electron loss/ gain.

statementText.2.2.1(a): the number of electrons that can fill the first four shells
statementText.2.2.1(b)(i): as a region around the nucleus that can hold up to two electrons, with opposite spins
statementText.2.2.1(b)(ii): the shapes of s- and p-orbitals
statementText.2.2.1(b)(iii): the number of orbitals making up s-, p- and d-sub-shells, and the number of electrons that can fill s-, p- and d-sub-shells
statementText.2.2.1(c)(i): for the first three shells and the 4s and 4p orbitals in order of increasing energy
statementText.2.2.1(c)(ii): for orbitals with the same energy, occupation singly before pairing
statementText.2.2.1(d): deduction of the electron configurations of:
statementText.2.2.1(d)(i): atoms, given the atomic number, up to Z = 36
statementText.2.2.1(d)(ii): ions, given the atomic number and ionic charge, limited to s- and p-blocks up to Z = 36.

name: Bonding, structure and shapes of molecules

statementText.2.2.2(a): ionic bonding as electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions, and the construction of 'dot-and-cross' diagrams
statementText.2.2.2(b): explanation of the solid structures of giant ionic lattices, resulting from oppositely charged ions strongly attracted in all directions e.g. NaCl
statementText.2.2.2(c): explanation of the effect of structure and bonding on the physical properties of ionic compounds, including melting and boiling points, solubility and electrical conductivity in solid, liquid and aqueous states
statementText.2.2.2(d): covalent bond as the strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms
statementText.2.2.2(e): construction of ‘dot-and-cross ’ diagrams of molecules and ions to describe:
statementText.2.2.2(f): use of the term average bond enthalpy as a measurement of covalent bond strength
statementText.2.2.2(g): the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules and ions with up to six electron pairs (including lone pairs) surrounding the central atom as predicted by electron pair repulsion, including the relative repulsive strengths of bonded pairs and lone pairs of electrons
statementText.2.2.2(h): electron pair repulsion to explain the following shapes of molecules and ions: linear, non-linear, trigonal planar, pyramidal, tetrahedral and octahedral
statementText.2.2.2(i): electronegativity as the ability of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond; interpretation of Pauling electronegativity values
statementText.2.2.2(j)(i): a polar bond and permanent dipole within molecules containing covalently-bonded atoms with different electronegativities
statementText.2.2.2(j)(ii): a polar molecule and overall dipole in terms of permanent dipole(s) and molecular shape
statementText.2.2.2(k): intermolecular forces based on permanent dipole– dipole interactions and induced dipole– dipole interactions
statementText.2.2.2(l): hydrogen bonding as intermolecular bonding between molecules containing N, O or F and the H atom of –NH, –OH or HF
statementText.2.2.2(m): explanation of anomalous properties of H2O resulting from hydrogen bonding, e.g.:
statementText.2.2.2(m)(i): the density of ice compared with water
statementText.2.2.2(m)(ii): its relatively high melting and boiling points
statementText.2.2.2(n): explanation of the solid structures of simple molecular lattices, as covalently bonded molecules attracted by intermolecular forces, e.g. I2, ice
statementText.2.2.2(o): explanation of the effect of structure and bonding on the physical properties of covalent compounds with simple molecular lattice structures including melting and boiling points, solubility and electrical conductivity.

statementText.3.1.1(a): the periodic table as the arrangement of elements:
statementText.3.1.1(a)(ii): in periods showing repeating trends in physical and chemical properties (periodicity)
statementText.3.1.1(a)(iii): in groups having similar chemical properties
statementText.3.1.1(b)(i): the periodic trend in electron configurations across Periods 2 and 3 (see also 2.2.1 d)
statementText.3.1.1(b)(ii): classification of elements into s-, p- and d-blocks
statementText.3.1.1(c): first ionisation energy (removal of 1 mol of electrons from 1 mol of gaseous atoms) and successive ionisation energy, and:
statementText.3.1.1(c)(i): explanation of the trend in first ionisation energies across Periods 2 and 3, and down a group, in terms of attraction, nuclear charge and atomic radius
statementText.3.1.1(c)(ii): prediction from successive ionisation energies of the number of electrons in each shell of an atom and the group of an element
statementText.3.1.1(d)(i): metallic bonding as strong electrostatic attraction between cations (positive ions) and delocalised electrons
statementText.3.1.1(d)(ii): a giant metallic lattice structure, e.g. all metals
statementText.3.1.1(e): explanation of the solid giant covalent lattices of carbon (diamond, graphite and graphene) and silicon as networks of atoms bonded by strong covalent bonds
statementText.3.1.1(f): explanation of physical properties of giant metallic and giant covalent lattices, including melting and boiling points, solubility and electrical conductivity in terms of structure and bonding
statementText.3.1.1(g): explanation of the variation in melting points across Periods 2 and 3 in terms of structure and bonding (see also 2.2.2 o).

statementText.3.1.2(a): the outer shell s2electron configuration and the loss of these electrons in redox reactions to form 2+ ions
statementText.3.1.2(b): the relative reactivities of the Group 2 elements Mg → Ba shown by their redox reactions with:
statementText.3.1.2(c): the trend in reactivity in terms of the first and second ionisation energies of Group 2 elements down the group (see also 3.1.1 c)
statementText.3.1.2(d): the action of water on Group 2 oxides and the approximate pH of any resulting solutions, including the trend of increasing alkalinity
statementText.3.1.2(e): uses of some Group 2 compounds as bases, including equations, for example (but not limited to):
statementText.3.1.2(e)(i): Ca(OH)2in agriculture to neutralise acid soils

statementText.3.1.3(a): existence of halogens as diatomic molecules and explanation of the trend in the boiling points of Cl2, Br2and I2, in terms of induced dipole– dipole interactions (London forces) (see also 2.2.2 k)
statementText.3.1.3(b): the outer shell s2p5electron configuration and the gaining of one electron in many redox reactions to form 1– ions
statementText.3.1.3(c): the trend in reactivity of the halogens Cl2, Br2 and I2, illustrated by reaction with other halide ions
statementText.3.1.3(d): explanation of the trend in reactivity shown in (c), from the decreasing ease of forming 1– ions, in terms of attraction, atomic radius and electron shielding
statementText.3.1.3(e): explanation of the term disproportionation as oxidation and reduction of the same element, illustrated by:
statementText.3.1.3(e)(i): the reaction of chlorine with water as used in water treatment
statementText.3.1.3(e)(ii): the reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide, as used to form bleach
statementText.3.1.3(e)(iii): reactions analogous to those specified in (i) and (ii)
statementText.3.1.3(f): the benefits of chlorine use in water treatment (killing bacteria) contrasted with associated risks (e.g. hazards of toxic chlorine gas and possible risks from formation of chlorinated hydrocarbons)
statementText.3.1.3(g): the precipitation reactions, including ionic equations, of the aqueous anions Cl–, Br– and I– with aqueous silver ions, followed by aqueous ammonia, and their use as a test for different halide ions.

statementText.3.1.4(a): qualitative analysis of ions on a test-tube scale; processes and techniques needed to identify the following ions in an unknown compound:
statementText.3.1.4(a)(i): anions: • CO32–, by reaction with H+(aq) forming CO2(g) (see 2.1.4 c) • SO42–, by precipitation with Ba2+(aq) • Cl–, Br–, I– (see 3.1.3 g)
statementText.3.1.4(a)(ii): cations: NH4+, by reaction with warm NaOH(aq) forming NH3.
statementText.5.3.2(a): qualitative analysis of ions on a test-tube scale: processes and techniques needed to identify the following ions in an unknown compound:
statementText.5.3.2(a)(i): anions: CO32–, Cl–, Br–, I–, SO42– (see 3.1.4 a)
statementText.5.3.2(a)(ii): cations: NH4+; Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Mn2+, Cr3+ (see 3.1.4 a, 5.3.1 j).

statementText.3.2.1(a): explanation that some chemical reactions are accompanied by enthalpy changes that are exothermic (∆H, negative) or endothermic (∆H, positive)
statementText.3.2.1(b): construction of enthalpy profile diagrams to show the difference in the enthalpy of reactants compared with products
statementText.3.2.1(c): qualitative explanation of the term activation energy, including use of enthalpy profile diagrams
statementText.3.2.1(d): explanation and use of the terms:
statementText.3.2.1(d)(i): standard conditions and standard states (physical states under standard conditions)
statementText.3.2.1(d)(ii): enthalpy change of reaction (enthalpy change associated with a stated equation, ∆rH)
statementText.3.2.1(d)(iii): enthalpy change of formation (formation of 1 mol of a compound from its elements, ∆fH)
statementText.3.2.1(d)(iv): enthalpy change of combustion (complete combustion of 1 mol of a substance, ∆cH)
statementText.3.2.1(d)(v): enthalpy change of neutralisation (formation of 1 mol of water from neutralisation, ∆neutH)
statementText.3.2.1(e): determination of enthalpy changes directly from appropriate experimental results, including use of the relationship: q = mc∆T
statementText.3.2.1(f)(i): explanation of the term average bond enthalpy (as the breaking of 1 mol of bonds in gaseous molecules)
statementText.3.2.1(f)(ii): explanation of exothermic and endothermic reactions in terms of enthalpy changes associated with the breaking and making of chemical bonds
statementText.3.2.1(f)(iii): use of average bond enthalpies to calculate enthalpy changes and related quantities (see also 2.2.2 f)
statementText.3.2.1(g): Hess’ law for construction of enthalpy cycles and calculations to determine indirectly:
statementText.3.2.1(g)(i): an enthalpy change of reaction from enthalpy changes of combustion
statementText.3.2.1(g)(ii): an enthalpy change of reaction from enthalpy changes of formation
statementText.3.2.1(g)(iii): enthalpy changes from unfamiliar enthalpy cycles
statementText.3.2.1(h): the techniques and procedures used to determine enthalpy changes directly and indirectly.

name: Reaction rates and the Boltzmann distribution

statementText.3.2.2(a): the effect of concentration, including the pressure of gases, on the rate of a reaction, in terms of frequency of collisions
statementText.3.2.2(b): calculation of reaction rate from the gradients of graphs measuring how a physical quantity changes with time
statementText.3.2.2(c): explanation of the role of a catalyst:
statementText.3.2.2(c)(i): in increasing reaction rate without being used up by the overall reaction
statementText.3.2.2(c)(ii): in allowing a reaction to proceed via a different route with lower activation energy, as shown by enthalpy profile diagrams
statementText.3.2.2(d)(i): explanation of the terms homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts
statementText.3.2.2(d)(ii): explanation that catalysts have great economic importance and benefits for increased sustainability by lowering temperatures and reducing energy demand from combustion of fossil fuels with resulting reduction in CO2emissions
statementText.3.2.2(e): the techniques and procedures used to investigate reaction rates including the measurement of mass, gas volumes and time
statementText.3.2.2(f): qualitative explanation of the Boltzmann distribution and its relationship with activation energy (see also 3.2.1 c)
statementText.3.2.2(g): explanation, using Boltzmann distributions, of the qualitative effect on the proportion of molecules exceeding the activation energy and hence the reaction rate, for:

statementText.3.2.3(a): explanation that a dynamic equilibrium exists in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction and the concentrations of reactants and products do not change
statementText.3.2.3(b): le Chatelier’s principle and its application for homogeneous equilibria to deduce qualitatively the effect of a change in temperature, pressure or concentration on the position of equilibrium
statementText.3.2.3(c): explanation that a catalyst increases the rate of both forward and reverse reactions in an equilibrium by the same amount resulting in an unchanged position of equilibrium
statementText.3.2.3(d): the techniques and procedures used to investigate changes to the position of equilibrium for changes in concentration and temperature.
statementText.3.2.3(e): explanation of the importance to the chemical industry of a compromise between chemical equilibrium and reaction rate in deciding the operational conditions
statementText.3.2.3(f): expressions for the equilibrium constant, Kc, for homogeneous reactions and calculations of the equilibrium constant, Kc, from provided equilibrium concentrations
statementText.3.2.3(g): estimation of the position of equilibrium from the magnitude of Kc.

name: Organic basics: naming, formulae and isomerism

statementText.4.1.1(a): application of IUPAC rules of nomenclature for systematically naming organic compounds
statementText.4.1.1(b): interpretation and use of the terms:
statementText.4.1.1(b)(i): general formula (the simplest algebraic formula of a member of a homologous series) e.g. for an alkane: CnH2n+2
statementText.4.1.1(b)(ii): structural formula (the minimal detail that shows the arrangement of atoms in a molecule) e.g. for butane: CH3CH2CH2CH3or CH3(CH2)2CH3
statementText.4.1.1(b)(iii): displayed formula (the relative positioning of atoms and the bonds between them) e.g. for ethanol: H H H C C O H H H
statementText.4.1.1(b)(iv): skeletal formula (the simplified organic formula, shown by removing hydrogen atoms from alkyl chains, leaving just a carbon skeleton and associated functional groups) e.g. for butan-2-ol: OH
statementText.4.1.1(c): interpretation and use of the terms:
statementText.4.1.1(c)(i): homologous series (a series of organic compounds having the same functional group but with each successive member differing by CH2)
statementText.4.1.1(c)(ii): functional group (a group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of a compound)
statementText.4.1.1(c)(iv): aliphatic (a compound containing carbon and hydrogen joined together in straight chains, branched chains or non-aromatic rings)
statementText.4.1.1(c)(v): alicyclic (an aliphatic compound arranged in non-aromatic rings with or without side chains)
statementText.4.1.1(c)(vi): aromatic (a compound containing a benzene ring)
statementText.4.1.1(c)(vii): saturated (single carbon– carbon bonds only) and unsaturated (the presence of multiple carbon– carbon bonds, including C=C, C/C and aromatic rings)
statementText.4.1.1(d): use of the general formula of a homologous series to predict the formula of any member of the series
statementText.4.1.1(e): explanation of the term structural isomers (compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae) and determination of possible structural formulae of an organic molecule, given its molecular formula
statementText.4.1.1(f): the different types of covalent bond fission:
statementText.4.1.1(f)(i): homolytic fission (in terms of each bonding atom receiving one electron from the bonded pair, forming two radicals)
statementText.4.1.1(f)(ii): heterolytic fission (in terms of one bonding atom receiving both electrons from the bonded pair)
statementText.4.1.1(g): the term radical (a species with an unpaired electron) and use of ‘dots’ to represent species that are radicals in mechanisms
statementText.4.1.1(h): a ‘curly arrow’ described as the movement of an electron pair, showing either heterolytic fission or formation of a covalent bond
statementText.4.1.1(i): reaction mechanisms, using diagrams, to show clearly the movement of an electron pair with ‘curly arrows’ and relevant dipoles.

statementText.4.1.2(a): alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons containing single C–C and C–H bonds as σ-bonds (overlap of orbitals directly between the bonding atoms); free rotation of the σ-bond
statementText.4.1.2(b): explanation of the tetrahedral shape and bond angle around each carbon atom in alkanes in terms of electron pair repulsion (see also 2.2.2 g– h)
statementText.4.1.2(c): explanation of the variations in boiling points of alkanes with different carbon-chain length and branching, in terms of induced dipole– dipole interactions (London forces) (see also 2.2.2 k)
statementText.4.1.2(d): the low reactivity of alkanes with many reagents in terms of the high bond enthalpy and very low polarity of the σ-bonds present (see also 2.2.2 j)
statementText.4.1.2(e): complete combustion of alkanes, as used in fuels, and the incomplete combustion of alkane fuels in a limited supply of oxygen with the resulting potential dangers from CO
statementText.4.1.2(f): the reaction of alkanes with chlorine and bromine by radical substitution using ultraviolet radiation, including a mechanism involving homolytic fission and radical reactions in terms of initiation, propagation and termination (see also 4.1.1 f– g)
statementText.4.1.2(g): the limitations of radical substitution in synthesis by the formation of a mixture of organic products, in terms of further substitution and reactions at different positions in a carbon chain.

statementText.4.1.3(a): alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a C=C bond comprising a π-bond (sideways overlap of adjacent p-orbitals above and below the bonding C atoms) and a σ-bond (overlap of orbitals directly between the bonding atoms) (see also 4.1.2 a); restricted rotation of the π-bond
statementText.4.1.3(b): explanation of the trigonal planar shape and bond angle around each carbon in the C=C of alkenes in terms of electron pair repulsion (see also 2.2.2 g– h, 4.1.2 b)
statementText.4.1.3(c)(i): explanation of the terms: • stereoisomers (compounds with the same structural formula but with a different arrangement in space) • E/Z isomerism (an example of stereoisomerism, in terms of restricted rotation about a double bond and the requirement for two different groups to be attached to each carbon atom of the C=C group) • cis– trans isomerism (a special case of E/Z isomerism in which two of the substituent groups attached to each carbon atom of the C=C group are the same)
statementText.4.1.3(c)(ii): use of Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) priority rules to identify the E and Z stereoisomers
statementText.4.1.3(d): determination of possible E/Z or cis– trans stereoisomers of an organic molecule, given its structural formula
statementText.4.1.3(e): the reactivity of alkenes in terms of the relatively low bond enthalpy of the π-bond
statementText.4.1.3(f)(i): hydrogen in the presence of a suitable catalyst, e.g. Ni, to form alkanes
statementText.4.1.3(f)(ii): halogens to form dihaloalkanes, including the use of bromine to detect the presence of a double C=C bond as a test for unsaturation in a carbon chain
statementText.4.1.3(f)(iv): steam in the presence of an acid catalyst, e.g. H3PO4, to form alcohols
statementText.4.1.3(g): definition and use of the term electrophile (an electron pair acceptor)
statementText.4.1.3(h): the mechanism of electrophilic addition in alkenes by heterolytic fission (see also 4.1.1 h– i)
statementText.4.1.3(i): use of Markownikoff’s rule to predict formation of a major organic product in addition reactions of H–X to unsymmetrical alkenes, e.g. H–Br to propene, in terms of the relative stabilities of carbocation intermediates in the mechanism
statementText.4.1.3(j): addition polymerisation of alkenes and substituted alkenes, including:
statementText.4.1.3(j)(i): the repeat unit of an addition polymer deduced from a given monomer
statementText.4.1.3(j)(ii): identification of the monomer that would produce a given section of an addition polymer
statementText.4.1.3(k): the benefits for sustainability of processing waste polymers by:
statementText.4.1.3(k)(ii): use as an organic feedstock for the production of plastics and other organic chemicals
statementText.4.1.3(k)(iii): removal of toxic waste products, e.g. removal of HCl formed during disposal by combustion of halogenated plastics (e.g. PVC)
statementText.4.1.3(l): the benefits to the environment of development of biodegradable and photodegradable polymers.

statementText.4.2.1(a)(i): the polarity of alcohols and an explanation, in terms of hydrogen bonding, of the water solubility and the relatively low volatility of alcohols compared with alkanes (see also 2.2.2 l and 4.1.2 c)
statementText.4.2.1(a)(ii): classification of alcohols into primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
statementText.4.2.1(c): oxidation of alcohols by an oxidising agent, e.g. Cr2O72–/H+(i.e. K2Cr2O7/H2SO4), including:
statementText.4.2.1(c)(i): the oxidation of primary alcohols to form aldehydes and carboxylic acids; the control of the oxidation product using different reaction conditions
statementText.4.2.1(c)(ii): the oxidation of secondary alcohols to form ketones
statementText.4.2.1(c)(iii): the resistance to oxidation of tertiary alcohols
statementText.4.2.1(d): elimination of H2O from alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g. H3PO4or H2SO4) and heat to form alkenes
statementText.4.2.1(e): substitution with halide ions in the presence of acid (e.g. NaBr/H2SO4) to form haloalkanes.

statementText.4.2.2(a): hydrolysis of haloalkanes in a substitution reaction:
statementText.4.2.2(a)(ii): by water in the presence of AgNO3and ethanol to compare experimentally the rates of hydrolysis of different carbon– halogen bonds
